Your man hour rate is the foundation of pricing discipline. It's not what you think you can charge—it's what you must make per hour to stay profitable as a business entity. As Caleb Allman explains in the episode , the difference between successful and struggling lawn care owners comes down to whether they've calculated and tracked this number religiously. The Employee-to-Owner Pricing Trap

When you work as an employee, someone else absorbs the true cost of running the business—insurance premiums, payroll processing, equipment depreciation, facilities, taxes. You only see your hourly wage. When you become a business owner, all those hidden costs suddenly become your responsibility , yet your pricing often doesn't reflect them.

A new lawn care owner thinks: "I was making $15/hour as an employee. Now I'm charging clients $50/hour. I'm making over three times as much—I'm successful." But that math ignores the fact that not all of your $50/hour becomes take-home profit . After subtracting payroll taxes (if you hire help), workers' compensation, equipment maintenance, fuel, replacement of worn-out tools, and business overhead, that $50 shrinks dramatically.

When speed and fatigue become profit limiters

The core decision is straightforward: equipment should pay for itself through efficiency gains. A walk-behind mower requires constant operator input and causes fatigue over long workdays, which slows job completion and forces you to budget more hours per project than faster equipment would require.

Zero-turn mowers deliver three concrete advantages. First, they complete yards faster than walk-behinds due to higher ground speed and tighter turning radius. Second, they reduce operator fatigue, meaning your crew stays productive through full shifts without performance degradation. Third, they eliminate the inefficiency of velcro-style attachments on walk-behinds that require manual setup and adjustments between tasks.

f: Start by defining your target man-hour rate—the amount you want to earn per person working per hour. Multiply that rate by the total number of man-hours required for a job to find your baseline charge. But you must add a buffer above this break-even number to cover overhead costs and operational inefficiencies; the final price should always exceed the basic man-hour calculation.
The Man-Hour Formula: From Theory to Job Pricing

A man-hour is one person working for one hour . If three crew members work one hour on a project, that job consumes three man-hours of labor. The math is straightforward: if your target rate is $100 per man-hour and a job requires three man-hours, your minimum charge is $300.

This approach works even if you never tell your clients you charge by the hour, as discussed in the episode . Many lawn care owners quote flat fees per project instead—but the underlying economics still run on hourly rates.
Why Your Quote Must Exceed the Break-Even Number

The $300 figure in our three-person example is only the bare minimum to cover labor costs . It doesn't account for your business overhead: truck fuel, equipment maintenance, insurance, office staff, scheduling inefficiencies, or the time you spend managing jobs instead of working on them.
